cards.q: Explain why atomic radius increases down Group 2 from magnesium to barium.
cards.a: Each element has one more shell of electrons.
marks: Each successive element has an extra electron shell.
The outer electrons are further from the nucleus.
Extra inner shells add shielding, which outweighs the increase in nuclear charge.

cards.q: Explain why the first ionisation energy decreases down Group 2.
cards.a: The outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded.
marks: Atomic radius increases: the outer electrons are in a higher shell, further from the nucleus.
There is more shielding by inner electrons.
This outweighs the increased nuclear charge, so the outer electron is attracted less strongly and is easier to remove.

cards.q: Describe and explain the general trend in melting point of the Group 2 elements.
cards.a: Melting point generally decreases down the group.
cards.why: The metal ions get larger, so the delocalised electrons are further from the nuclei; the metallic bonding (attraction between ions and delocalised electrons) is weaker.

cards.q: Magnesium melts at a lower temperature than calcium. Why does this not contradict the explanation for the Group 2 melting point trend?
cards.a: Magnesium’s metal lattice has a different crystal structure from calcium’s, so the two are not a like-for-like comparison. From calcium to barium the melting point does decrease.
cards.why: Trends based on ion size compare like with like; a change in lattice structure changes how the ions pack.

cards.q: Explain why the reactivity of the Group 2 elements increases down the group.
cards.a: The atoms lose their two outer electrons more easily, forming \(\mathrm{M^{2+}}\) ions.
marks: Group 2 elements react by losing their two outer electrons.
Down the group, atomic radius and shielding increase.
So the outer electrons are less strongly attracted to the nucleus.
The sum of the first and second ionisation energies decreases, so the ions form more easily.

cards.q: True or false: Group 2 metals become more reactive down the group because they gain electrons more easily.
cards.a: False. Group 2 metals lose electrons.
cards.why: They are reducing agents: they are oxidised from 0 to +2. Reactivity rises because the electrons are lost more easily.

cards.q: Write the general equation for a Group 2 metal M (Ca to Ba) reacting with water.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{M(s) + 2H_{2}O(l) \rightarrow M(OH)_{2}(aq) + H_{2}(g)}\)
cards.why: Calcium, strontium and barium react with cold water with increasing vigour down the group.

cards.q: Describe what you see when calcium is added to cold water.
cards.a: Fizzing (hydrogen), the calcium sinks and slowly disappears, the mixture warms up and goes cloudy white.
cards.why: The cloudiness is calcium hydroxide, which is only slightly soluble, coming out of solution.

cards.q: How does the reaction of magnesium with steam differ from its reaction with cold water?
cards.a:
Steam: rapid, burning with a bright white flame, forming magnesium oxide: \(\mathrm{Mg + H_{2}O \rightarrow MgO + H_{2}}\).
Cold water: very slow, forming magnesium hydroxide.
cards.why: At high temperature the hydroxide is not formed: magnesium oxide and hydrogen are produced.

cards.q: Write the general equation for a Group 2 metal burning in oxygen. What does magnesium look like as it burns?
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{2M(s) + O_{2}(g) \rightarrow 2MO(s)}\)
Magnesium burns with a brilliant white flame, forming a white powder.
cards.why: Group 2 oxides are white ionic solids. Barium burnt in excess oxygen also forms some barium peroxide.

cards.q: Write the equation for a Group 2 metal M reacting with chlorine.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{M(s) + Cl_{2}(g) \rightarrow MCl_{2}(s)}\)
cards.why: The metal is oxidised to \(\mathrm{M^{2+}}\); chlorine is reduced to \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\). The chlorides are white ionic solids.

cards.q: Write the equation for calcium oxide reacting with water. What is the trend in the pH of the solutions formed by Group 2 oxides?
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{CaO(s) + H_{2}O(l) \rightarrow Ca(OH)_{2}(aq)}\)
The solutions become more alkaline down the group.
cards.why: The hydroxides get more soluble down the group, so more hydroxide ions are in solution. The reaction of CaO is very exothermic.

cards.q: Write equations for magnesium oxide and for calcium hydroxide reacting with dilute hydrochloric acid.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{MgO(s) + 2HCl(aq) \rightarrow MgCl_{2}(aq) + H_{2}O(l)}\)
\(\mathrm{Ca(OH)_{2}(aq) + 2HCl(aq) \rightarrow CaCl_{2}(aq) + 2H_{2}O(l)}\)
cards.why: Group 2 oxides and hydroxides are bases: with acids they form a salt and water.

cards.q: Write the ionic equation for any Group 2 oxide reacting with an acid.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{O^{2-}(s) + 2H^{+}(aq) \rightarrow H_{2}O(l)}\)
cards.why: For a hydroxide in solution it is simply \(\mathrm{H^{+}(aq) + OH^{-}(aq) \rightarrow H_{2}O(l)}\).

cards.q: Why does the reaction of calcium oxide with dilute sulfuric acid soon slow down and stop, but not its reaction with dilute hydrochloric acid?
cards.a: Calcium sulfate is only sparingly soluble, so it forms a coating on the solid that stops the acid reaching it. Calcium chloride is soluble.
cards.why: This is worse still for strontium and barium, whose sulfates are even less soluble.

cards.q: State the trend in solubility of the Group 2 hydroxides.
cards.a: Solubility increases down the group. \(\mathrm{Mg(OH)_{2}}\) is sparingly soluble; \(\mathrm{Ba(OH)_{2}}\) is the most soluble.
cards.why: Hydroxides: solubility goes up the further down you go.

cards.q: State the trend in solubility of the Group 2 sulfates.
cards.a: Solubility decreases down the group. \(\mathrm{MgSO_{4}}\) is soluble; \(\mathrm{BaSO_{4}}\) is insoluble.
cards.why: The opposite of the hydroxide trend.

cards.q: True or false: barium hydroxide and barium sulfate are both insoluble in water.
cards.a: False. \(\mathrm{Ba(OH)_{2}}\) is the most soluble Group 2 hydroxide; \(\mathrm{BaSO_{4}}\) is insoluble.
cards.why: The two trends run in opposite directions, so barium is at the soluble end for hydroxides and the insoluble end for sulfates.

cards.q: Dilute sodium hydroxide is added to separate solutions of \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\), \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\), \(\mathrm{Sr^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}\). What is seen?
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\): white precipitate.
\(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\): slight white precipitate.
\(\mathrm{Sr^{2+}}\): very slight (or no) precipitate.
\(\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}\): no precipitate.
cards.why: The less soluble the hydroxide, the more precipitate forms: \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}(aq) + 2OH^{-}(aq) \rightarrow Mg(OH)_{2}(s)}\).

cards.q: Dilute sulfuric acid is added to separate solutions of \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\), \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\), \(\mathrm{Sr^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}\). What is seen?
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\): no precipitate.
\(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\): slight white precipitate.
\(\mathrm{Sr^{2+}}\): white precipitate.
\(\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}\): thick white precipitate.
cards.why: The less soluble the sulfate, the more precipitate forms: \(\mathrm{Ba^{2+}(aq) + SO_{4}^{2-}(aq) \rightarrow BaSO_{4}(s)}\).

cards.q: Why is magnesium hydroxide used in indigestion remedies such as milk of magnesia? Write the equation.
cards.a: It is a base that neutralises excess stomach acid: \(\mathrm{Mg(OH)_{2} + 2HCl \rightarrow MgCl_{2} + 2H_{2}O}\)
cards.why: Being only sparingly soluble, it does not make the stomach strongly alkaline.

cards.q: An antacid tablet contains \(0.500\ \text{g}\) of \(\mathrm{Mg(OH)_{2}}\) (\(M_{\text{r}} = 58.3\)). Calculate the amount of hydrochloric acid it can neutralise.
cards.a: \(0.0172\ \text{mol}\)
cards.why: Each hydroxide ion neutralises one hydrogen ion, and each formula unit has two.

cards.q: Why do farmers spread calcium hydroxide (slaked lime) on fields? Write an ionic equation.
cards.a: To raise the pH of acidic soil so that crops grow well: \(\mathrm{OH^{-}(aq) + H^{+}(aq) \rightarrow H_{2}O(l)}\)
cards.why: Many crops, such as maize and cassava, grow poorly in soil that is too acidic.

cards.q: Write equations for the removal of sulfur dioxide from power-station flue gases using calcium oxide and using calcium carbonate.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{CaO(s) + SO_{2}(g) \rightarrow CaSO_{3}(s)}\)
\(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}(s) + SO_{2}(g) \rightarrow CaSO_{3}(s) + CO_{2}(g)}\)
cards.why: Sulfur dioxide is an acidic gas and the calcium compounds are bases. This reduces acid rain.

cards.q: Calculate the mass, in tonnes, of calcium carbonate (\(M_{\text{r}} = 100.1\)) needed to remove \(1.00\) tonne of sulfur dioxide (\(M_{\text{r}} = 64.1\)) from flue gases.
cards.a: 1.56 tonnes
cards.why: With a 1 : 1 ratio you can scale by the \(M_{\text{r}}\) values directly: \(1.00 \times \frac{100.1}{64.1}\).

cards.q: How is magnesium used in the extraction of titanium? Write the equation.
cards.a:
It reduces titanium(IV) chloride at high temperature, under an argon atmosphere:
\(\mathrm{TiCl_{4} + 2Mg \rightarrow Ti + 2MgCl_{2}}\)
cards.why: Magnesium is oxidised (0 to +2) and titanium is reduced (+4 to 0). Argon stops the hot metals reacting with oxygen and nitrogen.

cards.q: Calculate the minimum mass of magnesium needed to produce \(1.00\ \text{kg}\) of titanium. (\(A_{\text{r}}\): Ti 47.9, Mg 24.3)
cards.a: \(1.01\ \text{kg}\)
steps: \(\mathrm{TiCl_{4} + 2Mg \rightarrow Ti + 2MgCl_{2}}\): 2 mol Mg per mol Ti, so \(41.8\ \text{mol}\) Mg.
cards.why: Magnesium is costly to produce, which is one reason titanium is an expensive metal.

cards.q: Why can barium sulfate be swallowed safely as a “barium meal”, even though barium ions are toxic? What is it used for?
cards.a: It is insoluble, so it is not absorbed into the blood. It absorbs X-rays, so it shows up the outline of the gut on an X-ray image.
cards.why: Soluble barium compounds such as barium chloride must never be swallowed.

cards.q: Describe the test for sulfate ions and give the ionic equation for a positive result.
cards.a:
Add dilute hydrochloric acid, then barium chloride solution. A white precipitate shows sulfate ions:
\(\mathrm{Ba^{2+}(aq) + SO_{4}^{2-}(aq) \rightarrow BaSO_{4}(s)}\)
cards.why: Barium chloride is used because barium sulfate is insoluble.

cards.q: Explain why the barium chloride solution in the sulfate test is acidified, and why sulfuric acid must not be used to acidify it.
cards.a: The acid removes carbonate ions, which would also give a white precipitate.
marks: Carbonate ions would react with \(\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}\) to give a white precipitate of \(\mathrm{BaCO_{3}}\), a false positive.
Acid removes them: \(\mathrm{CO_{3}^{2-} + 2H^{+} \rightarrow CO_{2} + H_{2}O}\).
Sulfuric acid contains sulfate ions, so it would give a white precipitate whatever was being tested.

cards.q: Write the equation for the thermal decomposition of a Group 2 carbonate, using calcium carbonate as the example.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}(s) \rightarrow CaO(s) + CO_{2}(g)}\)
cards.why: All Group 2 carbonates decompose this way on heating, to the oxide and carbon dioxide.

cards.q: Write the equation for the thermal decomposition of magnesium nitrate. What would you see?
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{2Mg(NO_{3})_{2}(s) \rightarrow 2MgO(s) + 4NO_{2}(g) + O_{2}(g)}\)
Brown fumes of nitrogen dioxide; a white solid remains.
cards.why: All Group 2 nitrates decompose to the oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen.

cards.q: Write the equation for the thermal decomposition of sodium nitrate. How does it differ from a Group 2 nitrate?
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{2NaNO_{3}(s) \rightarrow 2NaNO_{2}(s) + O_{2}(g)}\)
It forms the nitrite and oxygen only: no brown nitrogen dioxide.
cards.why: Group 1 nitrates (except lithium) are more thermally stable and decompose less far.

cards.q: How do lithium carbonate and lithium nitrate decompose? Why is lithium different from the rest of Group 1?
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{Li_{2}CO_{3} \rightarrow Li_{2}O + CO_{2}}\)
\(\mathrm{4LiNO_{3} \rightarrow 2Li_{2}O + 4NO_{2} + O_{2}}\)
cards.why: \(\mathrm{Li^{+}}\) is very small, so it polarises the anion strongly, like a Group 2 ion. Other Group 1 carbonates do not decompose at Bunsen temperatures.

cards.q: State the trends in the thermal stability of the carbonates and nitrates of Groups 1 and 2.
cards.a: Thermal stability increases down each group. Group 1 compounds are more stable than the Group 2 compounds of the same period.
cards.why: More stable means a higher temperature is needed to decompose the compound.

cards.q: Explain why the thermal stability of the Group 2 carbonates increases down the group.
cards.a: The cation gets larger, so it polarises the carbonate ion less.
marks: Down the group, the cation (same 2+ charge) gets larger, so its charge density decreases.
A smaller cation with higher charge density polarises (distorts) the electron cloud of the large carbonate ion more.
This weakens the C–O bonds in the carbonate ion, so it breaks up into CO₂ and the oxide more easily.
Larger cations polarise less, so the carbonate needs a higher temperature to decompose.

cards.q: Explain why sodium carbonate is more thermally stable than magnesium carbonate.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\) has a lower charge and a larger radius than \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\), so it is less polarising.
marks: \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) has a greater charge and a smaller radius than \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\), so a higher charge density.
\(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) polarises the carbonate ion more, weakening its C–O bonds.
So \(\mathrm{MgCO_{3}}\) decomposes at a lower temperature; \(\mathrm{Na_{2}CO_{3}}\) does not decompose on Bunsen heating.

cards.q: \(2.00\ \text{g}\) of calcium carbonate (\(M_{\text{r}} = 100.1\)) is heated until it has fully decomposed. Calculate the mass of solid left.
cards.a: \(1.12\ \text{g}\)
cards.why: Heating to constant mass shows the decomposition is complete.

cards.q: Describe how to compare the thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates in the laboratory.
cards.a: Heat the same amount (in moles) of each carbonate in a boiling tube with a delivery tube leading into limewater. Time how long the limewater takes to turn cloudy.
cards.why: Keep the Bunsen flame, the distance from the flame and the volume of limewater the same. A longer time means a more stable carbonate.

cards.q: Describe how to compare the thermal stability of Group 1 and Group 2 nitrates in the laboratory.
cards.a: Heat the same amount (in moles) of each nitrate in a test tube in a fume cupboard. Time how long it takes for brown nitrogen dioxide to appear, or for enough oxygen to relight a glowing splint.
cards.why: Nitrogen dioxide is toxic, hence the fume cupboard. Group 1 nitrates (other than lithium) give no brown gas.

cards.q: Give the flame colours of lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium and caesium compounds.
cards.a:
Lithium: red (crimson).
Sodium: yellow-orange.
Potassium: lilac.
Rubidium: red-violet.
Caesium: blue-violet.
cards.why: The sodium colour is so intense it can mask others, so the wire must be clean.

cards.q: Give the flame colours of calcium, strontium and barium compounds. What about magnesium?
cards.a:
Calcium: orange-red (brick red).
Strontium: crimson (red).
Barium: pale (apple) green.
Magnesium: no colour.
cards.why: Strontium compounds give fireworks and flares their red colour; barium compounds the green.

cards.q: Explain how a metal compound produces a characteristic flame colour.
cards.a: Electrons are excited to higher energy levels, then fall back and emit light of particular frequencies.
marks: Heat energy promotes (excites) electrons in the metal ions to higher energy levels.
The electrons fall back to lower energy levels.
Energy is released as light, with frequency given by \(\Delta E = hf\).
The energy gaps are fixed for each element, so particular frequencies in the visible region give a characteristic colour.

cards.q: Why do magnesium compounds give no flame colour?
cards.a: The light emitted by magnesium is not in the visible region of the spectrum.
cards.why: The energy gaps for magnesium’s electron transitions correspond to frequencies outside the visible range, so no colour is seen.

cards.q: Describe how to carry out a flame test.
cards.a: Clean a nichrome (or platinum) wire by dipping it in concentrated hydrochloric acid and heating it until it gives no colour. Dip it in the acid again, then in the solid sample, and hold it in a hot, non-luminous (blue) Bunsen flame. Note the colour.
cards.why: The acid helps form volatile metal chlorides; cleaning removes traces of other metals, especially sodium.

cards.q: True or false: barium carbonate decomposes more easily than magnesium carbonate because barium is the more reactive metal.
cards.a: False. Barium carbonate is the more stable; it needs a higher temperature.
cards.why: Thermal stability depends on how strongly the cation polarises the anion; the large \(\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}\) ion polarises the carbonate ion least.

cards.q: True or false: a red flame always shows that a compound contains lithium.
cards.a: False. Lithium, strontium and calcium all give red or orange-red flames.
cards.why: Similar colours must be distinguished by their exact shade or by another test.
